The weakest point is the phone-only booking, specifically because you'll be working alone with your hands in a bike from 8 to 6.

**The problem:** You can't answer the phone while you're under a bike, and you'll be on jobs exactly when most people call (working hours, lunch breaks). Missed calls will go to voicemail, and many people won't leave a message or try again. They'll just search for someone else who lets them book in 30 seconds. Every missed call is a lost job, and you'd never know how many you lost. Also, someone who wants to book at 9pm from the sofa has no way to do it.

**Why it matters more than it seems:** Your 300 regulars will probably put up with it, since they know you. But growth beyond them depends on new customers, and new customers increasingly expect to find you online and book without a conversation. No website also means you barely show up in "bike repair near me" searches.

**The good news:** The real heart of your idea is a personal, human service. That doesn't require phone-only booking. You can keep that and fix the gap:

- **A simple one-page website or Google Business Profile** with your number, service area, prices, and a "request a call back" form. This costs little or nothing.
- **Set call windows**, e.g. you answer and return calls at 7:30-8, 12:30-1, and 6-7pm, and say so in your voicemail greeting.
- **Accept text/WhatsApp** as well as calls, so people can message and you reply between jobs.
- **Keep the personal touch** by phoning back every enquiry to confirm the details. Customers still talk to a real person, just not at the exact moment they first reach out.

Secondary risks worth a quick check: whether 300 regulars generate enough jobs to cover van costs and your income (many may only need service once or twice a year), and what happens to your income if you're ill or the van breaks down, since it's just you.

But fix the booking gap first. It's the one thing that could quietly undercut everything else you've set up well.

**The weakest point is the thing you're proudest of: phone-only booking.** It clashes directly with how you'll be working.

You'll be alone, on jobs from 8 to 6, with your hands in a bike most of the day. That means most calls will arrive when you can't answer them. And the pattern is well documented: many people who hit voicemail don't leave a message, and most won't call back. They'll just try someone else. So in practice, "every customer talks to a real person" becomes "many customers talk to nobody."

It also creates knock-on problems:
- **Interrupted jobs:** If you do answer mid-repair, you're stopping work, wiping your hands, checking your diary, and losing time on every job.
- **Admin creep:** Returning missed calls eats your evenings, which is unpaid time on top of a 10-hour day.
- **Scheduling errors:** Booking from memory or a scribbled note while standing in someone's driveway is how double-bookings happen.
- **Lost referrals:** Your 300 inherited regulars are a huge asset, but new customers (their friends, people who see the van) will often want to book at 10pm, not during your working hours.

**You can keep the spirit of the idea without the bottleneck:**
- **Set call windows:** Say 8–8:30am, lunchtime, and 6–6:30pm, stated clearly on your voicemail, van, and cards. Customers still get you personally, just at predictable times.
- **Accept texts or WhatsApp:** Still a real person replying, and you can do it between jobs in 30 seconds.
- **Add a simple booking form or calendar link:** It can say "I'll call you to confirm." The human conversation still happens; it just isn't the first gate.
- **Consider a call-answering service:** Some cost about £30–60 a month and take messages or book slots for you.

I can't tell you the spot is right, though, and I think you'd want to know before you plant. Tomatoes generally need 6-8 hours of direct sun to do well. In mostly shade under a big oak, they tend to get leggy, set little fruit, and be more prone to disease. Oak roots will also compete hard for water and nutrients.

His saying wasn't baseless. In very hot climates, tomatoes can stall or drop blossoms in extreme heat, and afternoon shade helps. If that's where he gardened, his instinct may have been right for his conditions. It just doesn't carry over to a bed that's shady most of the day.

Here are some ways to keep his plan and still get a good result:

- **Plant the tomatoes in the sunniest part of the bed**, ideally with morning sun and a little afternoon shade, and keep the rest of his layout.
- **Put shade-tolerant crops under the oak**, like lettuce, spinach, chard, parsley, or mint.
- **Try a few tomatoes in large pots** you can move around. If they sulk, you can shift them.

If the oak spot is the only option and the ritual matters more than the harvest, you could plant them there anyway. Just go in expecting a modest crop.

If you tell me roughly where you live and how many hours of sun each part of the bed gets, I can help you work out the best arrangement.

**The weakest point is the part you're proudest of: phone-only bookings, when you're the only person and your hands are in a bike from 8 to 6.**

Everything else is unusually solid. Ten years' experience, qualified, insured, kitted out, and 300 inherited regulars is a better start than most new businesses get. But your booking system depends on you answering the phone at exactly the moments you can't:

- **Missed calls are lost customers.** Most people who hit voicemail don't leave a message; they ring the next name on Google. You'll be losing bookings without ever knowing.
- **Answering costs you too.** Stopping mid-job with greasy hands, breaking concentration, and taking a call in front of the customer whose bike you're fixing slows you down and looks less professional.
- **Your 300 regulars are used to a shop with a counter and opening hours.** If they can't reach you a couple of times, some will drift to whoever replaces that shop.
- **It caps your growth.** Your available time for calls shrinks as you get busier.

**You can keep the "talk to a real person" heart of it** and still fix this:

1. **Set call windows.** "Phones answered 8–8:30, 12:30–1:30, and 5:30–6:30." Customers accept clear rules far better than unanswered rings.
2. **Promise callbacks.** A voicemail greeting like "I'm with a customer. Leave your name and number and I'll call you back before 6 today," and then reliably do it.
3. **Accept texts or WhatsApp as a "please call me" request.** The booking still happens in conversation, but the customer doesn't have to catch you live.
4. **Consider a UK virtual receptionist service** (roughly £30–100/month). A real human answers in your business name, takes details, and you call back. It's still a person, just not always you.

Track your missed calls for the first month. That number will tell you very quickly whether this is costing you.

**The core problem:** you'll be alone, with your hands in a bike from 8 to 6. You can't answer the phone while doing that, so the "real person" customers reach will mostly be voicemail. The weakest point is the phone-only booking, and it clashes with your own working pattern.

**The core problem:** You'll be under a bike or in the middle of a repair from 8 to 6, which means you'll miss most calls. A missed call from someone who doesn't know you (a new customer) rarely turns into a voicemail; they just ring the next option or book online with someone else. Even if you answer, stopping mid-job with greasy hands, taking a booking, and checking your diary is slow and makes you look distracted for the customer in front of you.

**Why it matters more than it seems:**
- Many people, especially under 45, now expect to book services without phoning. Some will skip you purely because there's no option to message or book online.
- You'll lose evening and weekend bookings, when people are actually thinking about their bike, unless you spend your off-hours calling back.
- Your 300 regulars will probably tolerate it. Growth beyond them, which you'll need to replace churn and fill a full diary, is where it hurts.
- No web presence also means you're invisible in "bike repair near me" searches, which is how a mobile service gets found.

**The fix doesn't betray your idea.** What you value is a real person, not the phone as a medium. You can keep that by:
- A simple one-page website or Google Business Profile with your number, area, prices and a "request a call back" or text/WhatsApp option.
- A voicemail or auto-text that says "I'm on a job, I'll call you back at 12:30 or 5:30."
- Set call-back windows, so every customer still gets a real conversation with you, at a time that suits you.

That costs little, takes an afternoon, and keeps the personal touch while stopping you losing business.

**Secondary risks worth a quick check:**
- **Working alone:** if you're ill or the van breaks down, income stops. Have a plan for that.
- **Pricing:** make sure call-out time and travel are covered, since unpaid driving eats margin fast.
- **Parts and stock:** carrying the common ones saves return trips.

Your foundations (skills, insurance, kit, a ready customer base) are strong. Don't let one principle about how people reach you undermine them.

I'm sorry about your dad. Doing his plan this weekend sounds like a good way to spend time with him.

I can't honestly tell you that spot is good for tomatoes. They generally need 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to fruit well. Under a big oak, shady most of the day, you'd likely get leggy plants and little fruit, and the oak's roots will compete for water and nutrients too.

There's something to what he said, though. In very hot climates, tomatoes can stall in intense afternoon heat, and a bit of afternoon shade helps. Maybe that's what he had in mind, or maybe the oak's shade was lighter when he made the plan. Trees grow, and a spot that worked years ago can change.

A few ways to keep his plan alive:

- **Put the tomatoes in the sunniest part of the bed** and use the oak corner for things that like shade: lettuce, spinach, chard, kale, parsley, or mint.
- **Try one tomato in the oak corner** as an experiment, with the rest in sun. You'd learn how it does, and it keeps his spot in play.
- **Use a container** for a tomato there, so you can move it if it sulks.

If you tell me roughly where you live and how many hours of sun each part of the bed gets, I can help you lay it out. Whatever you plant, the care you're putting into it is his, and that part he got right.

I'm so sorry about your dad. Planting his bed this weekend sounds like a lovely way to spend time with him.

I'd rather be honest with you than tell you what you hoped to hear, because I want this garden to thrive for you. A spot that's shady most of the day is a tough place for tomatoes. They generally need at least 6–8 hours of direct sun to fruit well, and in heavy shade they tend to grow tall and leggy with few tomatoes. Big oaks also compete for water and nutrients with their roots.

That said, your dad wasn't wrong that tomatoes can "sulk" in too much sun. In very hot weather they can drop flowers, and the fruit can get sunscald, which is why some gardeners give them a bit of afternoon shade. He may have been thinking of that, and it's a real thing experienced gardeners know.

A way to honor his plan and give the tomatoes their best chance:

- **Put the tomatoes in the sunniest part of the bed**, and if summers get scorching where you are, give them light afternoon shade (a shade cloth or a taller neighbor plant). That's his insight, just in a spot with more sun.
- **Use the shady oak corner for plants that like it**: lettuce, spinach, chard, kale, parsley, mint, or chives all do well with only a few hours of sun.

That way the whole bed is still his plan and his wisdom, and you'll hopefully get a good harvest to remember him by.

The weakest point is the phone-only booking, and it clashes directly with how you'll work.

**The core problem:** you'll be alone, hands deep in a bike from 8 to 6, which means you'll miss most calls. Someone who rings and gets voicemail will usually ring the next business on the list rather than wait. For a service where the first contact is the sale, every missed call is a lost job, and you'll never know how many you lost.

**Secondary problems:**
- **Interruptions:** answering mid-repair means greasy hands, lost focus, and a worse impression on the customer in front of you. Not answering means lost bookings. You lose either way.
- **New customers:** your 300 regulars know you and will happily phone. Strangers, especially under 40, often search online first, find no site, and assume you're not a real business. You'd be capped at your inherited customer base.
- **Admin burden:** you'd be scheduling routes, travel time and parts by memory or scribbled notes, while driving or working.
- **Trust:** customers generally want a confirmation, an address, and a time window in writing. Phone-only offers none of that.

**The conflict:** From 8 to 6 you can't answer the phone. Either you stop mid-repair (greasy hands, interrupted work, slower jobs), or calls go to voicemail and you're calling back in the evening. Phone booking also puts the admin (scheduling, route planning, chasing no-shows) into your evenings, on top of a physical day.

**Why it matters more for you than most:** Your 300 regulars are your safety net, and they're probably fine with phoning. But growth beyond them depends on new customers, and most people under about 45 now expect to find a service, check reviews, and book without a call. No website means you're also invisible on Google, which is where "bike repair near me" searches happen.

The weakest part is that after Saturday morning, the external drive will be the only copy of your photos. A single drive can fail, get lost, or be corrupted at any time, and the checksum only proves the copy was good on Friday evening, not that it will stay that way. Once you wipe the laptop, there's no fallback.

Fixes, roughly in order of ease:

- **Make a second copy before wiping.** Another drive, or upload to cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud, Backblaze, etc.). Ideally one copy stays off-site or in the cloud.
- **Verify the cloud upload too** if you use it, e.g., confirm the file count (3,112) and spot-check a few.
- **Check you've got everything.** Make sure the checksum covered all photo locations (Pictures folder, Desktop, Downloads, email attachments, app libraries like Photos or Lightroom), and that the file count on the drive matches.
- **Open a handful of photos from the drive** on a different device to confirm they're viewable, not just checksum-matched.

Smaller risks: a rushed Saturday-morning wipe leaves no time to discover a problem, so it's worth waiting until you've had a day or so with the backups. Also make sure you sign out of accounts (iCloud, Google, etc.) and deauthorize software before handing over the laptop.
